question: What did liberals in nineteenth-century Europe mean by a 'representative, elected parliamentary government,' and why were they not considered 'democrats'?
ground_truth: Liberals argued for a representative, elected parliamentary government, subject to laws interpreted by a well-trained judiciary that was independent of rulers and officials. They were not democrats because they did not believe in universal adult franchise; they felt men of property mainly should have the vote, and they did not want the vote for women.

Early revolutionary laws made schooling compulsory for girls, made marriage a contract entered into freely, legalised divorce for both women and men, and allowed women to train for jobs. They were classed as passive citizens in 1791 and their clubs were banned during the Reign of Terror. Women in France won the right to vote in 1946.

These included the creation of state schools, making schooling compulsory for all girls, and allowing girls' fathers to no longer force them into marriage against their will. Women were also granted the right to divorce and could now train for jobs, become artists, or run small businesses. 

Women's struggle for equal political rights continued, but faced challenges. During the Reign of Terror, the new government banned women's political activities and arrested many prominent women. The example of the political activities of French women during the revolutionary years was kept alive as an inspiring memory. Women finally won the right to vote in France in 1946.

The period from 1793 to 1794 is referred to as the Reign of Terror. Robespierre followed a policy of severe control and punishment. Peasants were forced to transport their grain to the cities and sell it at prices ﬁxed by the government. The use of more expensive white ﬂour was forbidden; all citizens were required to eat the pain d’égalité (equality bread), a loaf made of wholewheat. Equality was also sought to be practised through forms of speech and address. The Society of Revolutionary and Republican Women was the most famous. Their main demand was that women enjoy the same political rights as men (the right to vote, to be elected to the Assembly and to hold political office). During the Reign of Terror the government ordered the closure of women's clubs and banned their political activities; many prominent women were arrested and a number executed.

During the Reign of Terror, the new government responded harshly to these demands. They issued laws ordering the closure of women's clubs and banning their political activities. Many prominent women were arrested and a number of them were executed.
